name: JavaScript Basics
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: Variables, coercion, functions, closures, array methods and async/await in modern JavaScript.

lesson.intro: JavaScript runs in every browser and on servers through Node.js. A handful of rules explain most of its surprises: how variables are scoped, how values get converted, how functions remember their surroundings, and how code that waits for something keeps running without blocking.

sections.title: let, const and var
sections.body:
JavaScript has three ways to declare a variable. Use `const` by default, `let` when the value must change, and avoid `var` in new code.

- `const` cannot be reassigned. It does not freeze the value: you can still push to a const array or change a property of a const object.
- `let` can be reassigned. Like `const`, it is block scoped: it exists only inside the nearest `{ }`.
- `var` is function scoped and hoisted. Its declaration moves to the top of the function, so reading it before the assignment gives `undefined` instead of an error.

Reading a `let` or `const` before its declaration line throws a ReferenceError. The stretch between the start of the block and the declaration is called the temporal dead zone.
sections.tip: Start with const. Switch to let only when you find you need to reassign.

check.question: You need a loop counter that goes up by one on each pass. Which declaration fits best?
check.explanation: The counter is reassigned, so const would throw. let allows reassignment and stays inside the loop block, while var leaks out of it and an undeclared name creates an accidental global.

sections.title: Types, coercion and equality
sections.body:
Values have types: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, `bigint`, `symbol` and `object` (arrays and functions are objects too). Variables have no type of their own; any variable can hold any value.

When an operator gets mixed types, JavaScript converts (coerces) one of them:

- `+` with a string joins text: `"5" + 1` is `"51"`.
- `-`, `*` and `/` convert to numbers: `"5" - 1` is `4`.

`==` coerces before comparing, which gives surprises like `0 == ""` being true. `===` compares without conversion, so values of different types are never equal. Use `===` and `!==`.

In an `if`, and with `&&`, `||` and `!`, every value counts as truthy or falsy. The falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN`. Everything else is truthy, including `"0"`, `"false"`, `[]` and `{}`.
sections.code:
console.log("5" + 1);     // 51  (a string)
console.log("5" - 1);     // 4   (a number)
console.log(0 == "");     // true  (coerced)
console.log(0 === "");    // false (different types)
console.log(Boolean([])); // true  (an empty array is truthy)
sections.tip: typeof null is "object", a historical bug. Check for null with value === null.

check.question: What does 3 === "3" evaluate to?
check.explanation: === does not convert types. A number and a string are never strictly equal, so the result is false. 3 == "3" would be true because == converts the string first.

sections.title: Functions, arrow functions and closures
sections.body:
A function declaration is hoisted, so you can call it before the line where it appears. Arrow functions are shorter and are usually stored in a `const`.

- With a single expression after `=>`, the value is returned automatically: `n => n * 2`.
- With braces, you need an explicit `return`.
- To return an object literal directly, wrap it in parentheses: `() => ({ ok: true })`. Without them the braces are read as a function body.
- Arrow functions do not get their own `this`; they use the `this` of the surrounding code.

A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, even after the outer function has returned. Each call to the outer function creates a fresh set of variables, so each returned function has its own private state.
sections.tip: Default parameters fill in missing arguments: function greet(name = "friend") { ... }.

check.question: Given const double = n => n * 2; what does double(4) return?
check.explanation: With no braces, an arrow function returns its expression, so it returns 4 * 2, which is 8. It would return undefined only if the body had braces and no return.

sections.title: Arrays, objects and array methods
sections.body:
Arrays hold ordered values (`items[0]` is the first). Objects hold named properties, read with `user.name` or `user["name"]`. The bracket form is needed when the key is in a variable.

Arrays and objects are stored by reference. Assigning one to another variable copies the reference, not the contents, so both names point at the same object. Use spread to make a shallow copy: `[...items]` or `{ ...user }`.

Three methods cover most array work, and none of them change the original array:

- `map(fn)` returns a new array with `fn` applied to each item.
- `filter(fn)` returns a new array with only the items where `fn` returns a truthy value.
- `reduce(fn, initial)` folds the array into one value. `fn(acc, item)` returns the next accumulator. Always pass the initial value: without it the first item becomes the starting accumulator, and an empty array throws a TypeError.

check.question: What does [3, 1, 2].map(n => n + 1) return?
check.explanation: map returns a new array with the function applied to each item, in the same order: 3 + 1, 1 + 1, 2 + 1. It does not sort or sum anything.

sections.title: Async basics: promises, async/await and the event loop
sections.body:
JavaScript runs your code on one thread. Slow work such as a network request or a timer is handed off, and your code keeps going. When the work finishes, a callback is queued.

The event loop runs queued callbacks only when the call stack is empty, which means after the current code has finished. Promise callbacks (`.then`, and the code after an `await`) go in the microtask queue, which is emptied before timer callbacks such as `setTimeout` run.

A promise is an object that stands for a value arriving later. It starts pending, then is either fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error.

- An `async` function always returns a promise, even when you `return` a plain value.
- `await` pauses that async function until the promise settles, then gives you the fulfilled value or throws the rejection error. Other code keeps running in the meantime.
- Wrap `await` in `try`/`catch` to handle rejections.

check.question: When does a setTimeout(fn, 0) callback run?
choices: Immediately, before the next line runs
After the current code finishes and pending promise callbacks have run
Exactly 0 ms later, interrupting whatever is running
Only after every other timer in the program has fired
check.explanation: A 0 ms timer only queues the callback. The event loop runs it once the call stack is empty and the microtask queue of promise callbacks has been drained. Nothing interrupts running code.

keyTerms.definition: A variable declared with let or const exists only inside the nearest pair of braces.
Declarations are processed before code runs, so var names and function declarations exist from the top of their scope.
Automatic conversion of a value to another type, such as "5" - 1 turning the string into a number.
Comparison that never converts types; values of different types are never equal.
A value treated as false in a condition: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined and NaN.
A function together with the variables from the scope where it was created, which it can still read and change later.
An object representing a value that will be available later; it is pending, then fulfilled or rejected.
The mechanism that runs queued callbacks one at a time whenever the call stack is empty.

summary: Use const by default and let when you must reassign; avoid var, which is function scoped and hoisted.
Use === so values are compared without coercion, and learn the short list of falsy values.
map, filter and reduce return new values and leave the original array alone; give reduce an initial value.
A closure keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was created.
async functions return promises, await pauses only its own function, and queued callbacks run after the current code finishes.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who knows a little programming why setTimeout(() => console.log("B"), 0) logs after the line below it, and what await does to the function it appears in.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: const stops you from pointing arr at a different array, but push changes the existing array in place, which is allowed. The TypeError only happens on a reassignment such as arr = [].

questions.question: This code throws an error. Why?
choices: for...of loops cannot declare their variable with const
count must be declared with var to be used inside a loop
count is const, so count = count + 1 is a reassignment and throws a TypeError
A number variable cannot count the items of a string array
questions.explanation: Reassigning a const throws TypeError: Assignment to constant variable, so count should be declared with let. The const in for...of is fine because each pass creates a new binding for item.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: var declarations are hoisted to the top of the script or function, but the assignment stays where it is. So total exists but has no value yet. With let or const the same code throws a ReferenceError.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: When either side of + is a string, + joins text. The number 1 becomes "1" and the result is the string "51", not the number 6.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: - only works on numbers, so the string "5" is converted to 5 and the result is the number 3. Only + switches to joining strings.

questions.question: Which comparison evaluates to false?
questions.explanation: === never converts types, and null and undefined are different types, so it is false. The other three use ==, which coerces: null and undefined are loosely equal to each other, and "" and "1" become the numbers 0 and 1.

questions.question: Which of these values is truthy?
questions.explanation: Any non-empty string is truthy, even "0". The number 0, the empty string and NaN are all on the falsy list. It is the string's length that matters, not what it says.

questions.question: Complete the arrow function so makeUser("Ada") returns the object { name: "Ada" }.
questions.explanation: Parentheses tell JavaScript the braces are an object expression to return. Without them, { name: name } is read as a function body containing a label, so the function returns undefined. { return name } returns the string, not an object.
questions.concept: returning an object from an arrow function

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: Each call to makeCounter creates a new count variable. a has been called three times by the time it is logged, so it returns 3; b has its own count and returns 1 on its first call. Separate calls of the outer function do not share state.

questions.question: This code should log 0, 1, 2 but logs 3, 3, 3. What is the fix?
choices: Use a longer delay so the loop has time to finish
Replace the arrow function with a regular function
Declare i with let so each iteration gets its own i for the callback to close over
questions.explanation: var creates one i for the whole loop. The callbacks run after the loop ends, when that shared i is 3. let creates a fresh binding on every iteration, so each callback remembers its own value. Changing the function style or the increment does not change how many i variables exist.

questions.question: Complete the code so total is the number 12.
questions.code:
const prices = [{ price: 5 }, { price: 7 }];
const total = prices.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, _____);
questions.explanation: The accumulator must start as the number 0 so each step adds numbers. Starting with "" or [] turns + into string joining and gives "57", and starting with prices[0] adds to an object, giving "[object Object]7".

questions.question: What array does this expression return?
questions.explanation: filter keeps the even numbers, giving [2, 4], then map multiplies each by 10. Chained methods run left to right, each on the array returned by the previous one.

questions.question: What does this code log?
questions.explanation: b = a copies the reference, so a and b point to the same object, and changing b.score changes the one object both names see. Changing a property of a const object is allowed; only reassigning the variable throws.

questions.question: In what order are the letters logged?
questions.explanation: Synchronous code runs first: A, then D. Then the microtask queue runs the promise callback C, and only after that does the event loop pick up the timer callback B, even though its delay is 0.

questions.question: This code logs undefined instead of Ada. What is wrong?
choices: getUser returns a Promise, so show must be async and use await getUser()
Objects returned from functions lose their properties
user.name must be written as user["name"]
getUser must call resolve() before it returns
questions.explanation: An async function always returns a promise. user is that promise, which has no name property, so user.name is undefined. Awaiting it inside an async function gives the object itself. resolve belongs to new Promise, not to async functions.

questions.question: Complete the code so res holds the response, not a pending promise.
questions.explanation: await pauses loadUser until the fetch promise settles and hands back its value, the response. async marks a function, not an expression, and yield belongs to generator functions.

questions.question: What does await do inside an async function, and does it block the rest of the program?
questions.answer: await pauses only that async function until the promise settles, then returns the fulfilled value or throws the rejection error. The rest of the program keeps running while it waits.
questions.explanation: await is not a busy wait. The function is suspended and resumed later from the microtask queue, so other code and callbacks can run in the meantime.
